https://www.dw.com/en/andrew-tate-brothe.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5HNCZ Prosecutors in the UK had requested the Tate brothers' extradition [FILE: February 2025] Image: Marta Lavandier/AP/picture alliance Advertisement US federal authorities arrested social media influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate . Brady McCarron, a spokesperson for the Marshals Service, told The Associated Press, which first reported on the arrest, that the warrant was sealed. Prosecutors in the UK said they sought the brothers' extradition on charges of rape and sex trafficking. "We have decided to prosecute Andrew and Tristan Tate for further offences including rape, arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation and offences relating to indecent images of a child," said Malcolm McHaffie, Head of the Special Crime Division at the Crown Prosecution Service. The offenses are alleged to have happened between July 2010 and August 2017, according to the CPS statement . What are the charges against the Tate brothers? The CPS is bringing the following charges: Andrew Tate, 39, with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and 19 additional charges for offences relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography Tristan Tate, 38, with one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation Joseph McBride, an attorney representing the Tate brothers, called the new charges "filth and slander" aimed at derailing defamation lawsuits filed by the brothers in the United States. "We are confident that once a competent judge sees the facts, and once the Department of Justice confronts this egregious abuse of its own authority, Andrew and Tristan Tate will walk free. America does not do Britain’s political dirty work," McBride said in a statement posted on X. Andrew Tate has amassed over 10 million followers on X [FILE: March 22, 2025] Image: Vadim Ghirda/AP/picture alliance What to know about Andrew Tate and his brother Andrew Tate first reached a mainstream audience after appearing on the UK reality show Big Brother in 2016, but he was removed when a video surfaced that appeared to show him assaulting a woman. The Tate brothers, dual US and British citizens who moved to Romania , were arrested there in 2022. They were accused of human trafficking and forming a criminal gang to sexually exploit women — allegations they denied. The case didn't go forward after a Romanian court found legal and procedural irregularities on the part of the prosecutors. Andrew and Tristan Tate, both former kickboxers, are often associated with the " manosphere ," a male-centered social media movement rooted in anti-feminist discourse. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y4.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Germany said the attack at Leipzig airport was part of a pattern of "Russian hybrid operations" in Europe By Sarah Rainsford Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent Published 23 minutes ago As summer temperatures in Europe smashed records this summer and many politicians shifted to holiday mode, Russia remained focused on its war. Not only did its military attacks across Ukraine intensify last month, becoming ever more deadly for civilians, Russia also appears to have escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe. This time, military and defence sector sites were the prime target. A full month after drones packed with explosives were found at Leipzig's airport, used by Ukraine to transport military goods, Germany's interior minister has declared that "Russia is responsible". Russia's President Vladimir Putin is demanding proof, as always, and his officials call the accusation "absurd". But the drones were just a dramatic start. August then brought a series of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia. Some of the affected countries have already blamed Russia; others are still investigating and some fires may eventually be ruled accidental, exactly as such attacks are designed to seem. Poland's interior minister is clear. "There are many, many signals that Russia is changing its strategy and intensifying its activities, including terrorist and sabotage activities," Marcin KierwiÅski said, warning people to be on their guard. Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack Published 2 days ago EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Germany Published 1 day ago August campaign across Europe 4 August Germany: The first drone at Leipzig airport is discovered. 10 August Bulgaria: A major fire breaks out at a factory of the defence firm EMCO, with initial reports that a truck ignited during a fuel delivery. 13 August Italy: A fire at KNDS Ammo Italy outside Rome triggers a large explosion. The local prosecutor is looking into possible outside interference, La Repubblica newspaper reports. Publicly, his office will only confirm that a case has been opened for negligent disaster against "unknown persons". 15 August Estonia: The Milrem Robotics factory in Tallinn, which the Kyiv Post says supplies drones to Ukraine, goes up in flames. Two suspects are arrested. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal says the possibility of Russian sabotage is being "taking seriously" by investigators. 25 August Slovakia: Police announce they have averted an arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer and seized a "large amount of incendiary mixture". The firm itself blames Russia and police arrest three suspects who they say were "following orders". Slovakia is Russia's close ally in Europe. 30 August Poland: A country which is heavily targeted for sabotage reports two more fires. One is in Lublin at a company which produces helicopter components. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said arson "cannot be ruled out". An attack on the drone producer, WB Group, is clearer cut. A masked man is caught on CCTV throwing incendiary devices. Tusk calls it a "continuation of Russia's escalatory activities". The pattern has continued into September with two Bulgarians arrested in Munich, Germany, for suspected arson after throwing incendiary devices from a car at defence firm Rhode & Schwartz. Image source, EPA Image caption, The 31 August fire at SkarÅ¼ysko-Kamienna targeted one of Poland's biggest defence firms Why is this happening now? Attacks on military and defence targets are not new, although previous acts of sabotage linked to Russia include more puzzling targets - such as an Ikea store and a Polish paint store. The novelty now is the concentration of cases. "The intensity of military sites being attacked we've seen over the past couple of weeks is unusual," Daniela Richterova of the Department of War Studies at King's College says. She links the spike to developments in Russia's invasion of Ukraine. "We've basically seen Ukraine take the war to Russia and strike deep inside Russian territoryâ¦They [Moscow] are under pressure, they have to do something." Whilst some sabotage is staged to sow chaos or fear, Richterova believes the Kremlin's aim right now is "coercive signalling": pressuring countries to stop supporting Kyiv by raising the stakes. After a slow start, Germany is Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. There are other theories. To some, Russia is less concerned about "turning off the taps" of supplies to Ukraine and more about testing Nato for weaknesses. "Russia is probing the boundaries of what's acceptable and collecting information on the results. They find out what works, and what's vulnerable," argues Keir Giles from the Chatham House think tank. He sees the sabotage campaign as preparation for the "next phase", as he puts it, of Russia's aggression in Europe. "They're assessing the willingness of the victim country to actually do something about it." The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), which tracks sabotage cases, points to a previous surge in 2024 when Ukraine's allies began allowing it to use Western-supplied weapons deeper inside Russia. 2024 was the year of the parcel bomb plot, when Russia was accused of sending packages containing liquid explosive to the UK and Poland. One ignited shortly before it was loaded on to a DHL cargo plane. It is thought this was a test run for something significantly bigger. Image source, Police handout Image caption, Four parcels were sent from Lithuania to the UK and Poland in 2024 - two caught fire, at a warehouse in the UK and at Leipzig's airport Inside the Russian explosives plot that sent incendiary parcels to the UK Published 11 March "That was a marked high in terms of their willingness to inflict mass casualties," Giles adds. It was a step so serious, the White House contacted the Kremlin to tell it to stop. Russia had probed and found the limit. But the attacks have continued. German media on Friday quoted a federal police report that lists more than 165 suspected sabotage cases nationwide this year, though they don't say who is responsible. Who are the suspected saboteurs? Reports from Germany suggest the men who loaded and launched the drones at Leipzig's airport were Russian, and at least one may have entered the country specially for this job. That would be unusual. The vast majority of sabotage attacks in Europe have been carried out by Russian proxies: its so-called "gig economy saboteurs". They are usually Russian-speakers from former Soviet states, recruited online and driven by the cash, not political conviction. In one case the BBC reported from Poland, the saboteurs-for-hire had previously fought for Ukraine as volunteers. The "handlers" are generally thought to remain in Russia, co-ordinating operations online. The IISS likened the proxies they used to kamikaze drones: cheap and easy to launch in large numbers, but disposable. The amateurs can be sloppy or reckless, though. In the parcel plot, one man failed to find a pick-up point and the whole mission had to be aborted. So if Moscow did send professionals for the Leipzig drone launch, it suggests it wanted precision - and success. In fact, the devices appear to have malfunctioned. Nato faced with Soviet-style campaign Russia's sabotage operations seem to come from the Cold War playbook. Daniela Richterova's research shows very similar targets on Soviet sabotage lists, and agents-saboteurs were used in much the same way. The idea, she says, was to have small, deniable attacks in peace-time that would escalate in times of war. "I think we are still in the grey zone between the two, but the kind of attacks we've seen in the past weeks shrink that zone," she says. "And I think that increases the risk of what happens next." As Nato scrambles to respond, questions like how many small, individual attacks add up to a sustained Russian assault - and demand action - remain unanswered. Perhaps riskier than all is the potential for escalation by accident. What if the exploding parcel had gone off mid-air and caused a crash? What if the Leipzig drone had brought down a plane? "I think it could result in a big attack," Richterova says. "Then Nato, in this heightened security environment, would not be able to ignore that, and have to react." https://www.politico.eu/article/macron-a.text: LONDON — French President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez have welcomed Andy Burnham’s plan to unpick Brexit. Speaking at a joint press conference on Wednesday, Macron said Britain returning to the EU would be “excellent ​news” ⁠while Sanchez said the U.K. would be welcomed “with open arms.” “This is very good news, both for his country and for Europeans,” Macron told reporters of the U.K. prime minister’s policy shift. “Welcome back.” Advertisement Advertisement Rejoining would be “a wise decision” and Burnham was “right to show such boldness,” Macron added. Speaking at the same press conference, Sanchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain's return with open arms.” Burnham told Labour’s conference in Liverpool yesterday that Brexit had done more “harm than good” and that he would lay out the “different options” available to repair the damage at a forthcoming U.K.-EU summit expected in November. Speaking to broadcasters the morning after the speech , the PM confirmed the options could include rejoining the single market, the customs union, or even going “all the way” and rejoining the EU entirely. But the U.K. prime minister’s announcement was met with a more muted response from Brussels itself. A European Commission spokesperson said: “The U.K. is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the U.K. Government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.” Advertisement Advertisement ‘We’ll wait for concrete proposals’ EU officials and diplomats, however, told POLITICO that behind the scenes the speech had been received positively in the European capital. “The mood is positive and commitment to have a good summit is definitely there,” said one EU official, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “There is a lot of work ongoing to prepare for it.” Diplomats say that reaction among other EU member countries has also so far been broadly positive — if somewhat wary. One EU diplomat wondered aloud whether Burnham’s grand about-face would undermine the rationale for the upcoming U.K.-EU summit — which is yet to get a date but which was meant to conclude talks on a number of side-deals begun by Keir Starmer. “Why bother with difficult negotiations on SPS, emission trading and youth mobility if the U.K. wants a completely new deal?” they said. A second EU diplomat said the speech had been positively received, but added: “The U.K. will have to decide for itself what it wants. We’ll wait for concrete proposals from London.” Advertisement Advertisement A third noted: “We will see what he says. It will most likely take longer than November [to discuss], probably some time next year.” Sandro Gozi, the MEP who chairs the European Parliament’s parliament's delegation to U.K., said that Burnham’s “call for a new course deserves a serious European response.” “Let’s turn that opening into concrete choices for a closer EU-U.K. partnership to give citizens and businesses on both sides of the channel a more prosperous, secure future,” he said.

Now, Mikołaj has turned his attention to electric propulsion , particularly the Audi A6 e-tron that, despite only having an official WLTP range of 482 miles on a single charge, managed to travel almost double that on a recent record-breaking journey. Starting at Zakopane, Poland, the endeavor saw the electrified A6 traverse the Tatra Mountains (handy for regenerative braking), travel to Kraków, then along the Vistula Valley to Sandomierz and finally to Hel (no, not that one). Latest Videos From TechRadar Watch full video here: Once in Hel, the pro driver turned around and started retracing his steps before the Audi A6 e-tron eventually conked out, having covered a mightily impressive 831.4 miles on a single charge. (Image credit: Audi) That's the same distance as driving from New York to Chicago or London to Milan without stopping at a charging station. You may like Forget range anxiety: this new EV claims 683 miles between charges Volkswagen sets three EV records and proves big batteries aren't everything I helped drive this record-setting EV across Britain for free on sunshine alone The exact model used in the attempt was the Audi A6 Sportback e-tron performance, which features a 326hp rear-mounted motor and a 100kWh gross battery capacity, which equates to a net usable capacity of 94.9 kWh. More impressively, the previous record holder, the Lucid Air Grand Touring , has a larger battery pack with a nominal capacity of 112kWh. According to Marczyk, many sections of the trip were carried out in rush hour traffic and at an average temperature of 15 degrees Celsius. However, at certain points, the mercury dropped to just seven degrees Celsius, proving that EVs can still perform in cold weather. Analysis: easy does it (Image credit: Audi) When looking at the official range figures of modern EVs , it is generally good practice to aim for a number that is 10-20% lower than the one advertised. What to read next Hyundai beats Tesla in world's biggest EV battery study over 500,000 tests I've driven the Audi RS 5 and it mixes supercar pace with cutting-edge tech I tested the Volvo EX60 and BMW iX3 — and range anxiety is officially dead Real-world driving eats into electric range, something that’s even more pertinent when tackling cold weather. But the recent Guinness World Record is proof that things can be flipped on their head with a spot of careful driving. Marczyk says that maximizing regenerative braking opportunities, regularly checking tire pressure, and reading the road to avoid any abrupt braking can massively increase the potential range of an EV’s battery. So next time you hear someone stressing about range anxiety, remind them that it might be their driving style that’s forcing all of those charging stops. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw3d.text: Image source, Social Media Image caption, The Flydubai flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia after passengers managed to take back the aircraft's controls By Simon Atkinson ,Â BBC Australia producer Â and Â Jaroslav Lukiv Published 7 hours ago The Omani co-pilot who allegedly attempted to hijack a Flydubai plane started a "drift towards extremism and terrorism" while studying in Australia, United Arab Emirates officials say. UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi also alleged the pilot - widely named as Hamam al-Hammami - was last week trying to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's airport in a "suicide attack". He wounded the captain in the cockpit with the emergency crash axe before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew on the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight was able to land the aircraft in Saudi Arabia. Melbourne university RMIT earlier confirmed the pilot had studied there but left before completing his engineering qualification. FlyDubai: What Happened? What began as a routine flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv turned into a fight for survival when one pilot allegedly stabs another inside the cockpit. Watch on iPlayer According to Shamsi, interrogations of the 29-year-old pilot revealed he had been inspired by al-Qaeda's 11 September attacks in the US in 2001. "The findings indicated that signs of his drift towards extremism and terrorism first emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia," the attorney-general was quoted as saying by the UAE's state news agency Wam on Friday. "During that period, he was influenced by takfiri [radical] ideology through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks." The Wam report also said the pilot had told investigators "he had prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach". "He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim," Wam said. The Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported the man was issued an Australian student visa in 2014 and studied in the country in 2015-17, before leaving. This week, the Sydney Morning Herald unearthed tweets from al-Mammami's now-deleted X account in which he referred to his five years spent studying abroad in Australia, Britain, and New Zealand, as "the golden years of my religious commitment". More than 170 passengers and crew were on board flight FZ1073 on 30 September. In the days after the incident, Australian authorities confirmed they were looking into the man's links to Australia. The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team - made up of the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Victoria Police and the country's security agency ASIO - said it was "investigating the man's links to Australia". Figure caption, Watch: Tearful pilot recounts moment of Flydubai attack Indian co-pilot Capt Smit Machchhar has been hailed a hero after managing to unlock the cockpit door while being violently attacked with an axe, allowing passengers to get in and take control of the aircraft. Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by Flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv. Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views. He was later hired by UAE-based Flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials. Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country.
